name: AngelTrax Mobile Video Surveillance Solutions

profile.address: 119, South Woodburn Drive, Dothan, Houston County, Alabama, 36305
profile.reading:
The building at this address, 119 South Woodburn Drive in Dothan, Alabama, is the corporate headquarters of AngelTrax, a manufacturer of mobile video surveillance and fleet-safety systems for school buses, mass transit, locomotives, and commercial fleets -- not a purpose-built or commercial data center in the ordinary sense this registry otherwise documents. AngelTrax's own site describes a company, operating since 2006, that builds in-vehicle cameras, stop-arm safety systems for school buses, driver-behavior analytics, and fleet-monitoring hardware, with roughly 250,000 active systems in the field worldwide and about 30,000 shipped annually. That same page does state that AngelTrax maintains what it calls a "SOC 2 Type II-compliant data center" at this headquarters location, describing it as the secure hosted video and data infrastructure behind its CJIS-compliant video-storage product for customers' recorded footage.

That claim is almost certainly why this location was tagged as a data center in the underlying map data, and it should be taken at face value as far as it goes: AngelTrax does host customer video data from company-owned infrastructure here. But it is an enterprise-private facility built to serve AngelTrax's own product, not a wholesale or colocation data center that leases capacity to outside tenants, and nothing in AngelTrax's public materials describes dedicated generator plant, a raised-floor server hall, or other purpose-built data center construction distinct from an office building with a server room inside it. No zoning case, building permit, or utility record specific to a data-center-scale power or cooling buildout has been found for this Woodburn Drive address, which is consistent with a corporate office housing IT infrastructure sized to the company's own hosted-video workload rather than a facility built around server capacity as its primary purpose.

AngelTrax itself is a real, active company serving the pupil-transportation and fleet-safety markets nationally from this Dothan base, and the hosted-video service it offers customers is a legitimate part of its business. The relevant point for this registry is narrower: this entry documents an enterprise's own internal hosting footprint attached to its headquarters, not a facility that markets data center space, and readers researching commercial data center capacity in the Dothan, Alabama area should not treat this listing as evidence of purpose-built colocation infrastructure at this address. Enterprise-private server rooms like this one are common and rarely publish specifications, because they were never built to be marketed -- that absence of a public spec sheet is itself the expected signature of this category of facility, not a research gap.

reading:
AngelTrax is the trading name of IVS, Inc., a Dothan, Alabama company that builds mobile video and fleet safety systems for school buses, transit agencies, paratransit operators and commercial fleets. It is not a data centre business. It appears in this registry because a single building in a Dothan office park was mapped with the tag telecom=data_center, given the name AngelTrax Data Center and described by the contributor as a cloud based services data centre for the company. That is the entire basis of the entry, and the page below is an attempt to say what is actually there.

The mapped building carries the address 118 South Woodburn Drive, while AngelTrax gives its own mailing address as 119 South Woodburn Drive, on the opposite side of the same short street. So the registry is either describing the company's own premises with a transposed house number, or a second building across the road that the company also uses. Nothing in the public record resolves which, and no assessor record, permit or company statement has been found that identifies a separate purpose built computing facility at either number.

What the company does say about its infrastructure is modest and consistent. AngelTrax sells a hosted service under which fleet video files, transportation data, driver behaviour records and access logs are stored on servers the company runs itself, and it markets that arrangement on the grounds that customer footage is never handed to a third party host. It states that the hosting sits in a SOC 2 Type II compliant United States data centre. It does not name the city, the building, the operator of that building or whether the space is owned, leased or colocated, and it publishes no floor area, rack count, power figure or redundancy design. It is entirely possible that the SOC 2 audited space is a commercial colocation cage somewhere else and that the Dothan building is a corporate office with a server room in it. The registry should not assert more than that.

There is a real reason a company of this kind keeps its own servers. Video from school buses and public transit is evidence. It gets subpoenaed, it supports insurance claims and disciplinary proceedings, and in many states it is subject to student privacy rules that make a chain of custody argument easier when the vendor can point to a single controlled environment. AngelTrax holds public sector contracts on that basis, including a Texas Department of Information Resources prime contract, number DIR-CPO-5281, for mobile digital video products and related services available to Texas state agencies, local governments, school districts and public safety bodies. Selling to that customer base is what makes an in house hosting story worth marketing.

None of the four power figures this registry tracks exists for the Dothan building. There is no stated critical IT load, no published utility service size, no generator count or standby rating and no on site generation. Anyone who encounters a capacity number attached to this operator should assume it was inferred rather than reported.

The wider point is about how registries like this one get built. A single volunteer map tag on an ordinary commercial building can create an operator record, a facility count and, downstream, an entry in a commercial directory that reads as though a data centre operator exists where none does. AngelTrax is a real company doing real work with real servers, but on the evidence available it belongs in this registry as an enterprise with captive hosting rather than as an operator of a data centre facility.
